1. Executive Overview

This comprehensive technical report documents the end-to-end mathematical formulation, empirical benchmarking, and rigorous comparative analysis of 44 distinct optimization algorithms and paradigms prescribed across Chapter 6 of the curriculum. Over an intensive 14-day cycle, ten specialized tracks spanning continuous optimization (gradient descent variants, adaptive step sizes, second-order Hessians, backpropagation), discrete combinatorial optimization (0/1 Knapsack, Max-Cut, QUBO, Ising formulations), quantum variational optimization (QAOA, VQE, QNN, noise models, barren plateaus), parallel and distributed systems (submodular coverage, work-stealing thread pools, FedAvg, multi-task gradient balancing), real-world systems engineering (Electric Vehicle VRPTW fleet routing), systems software (compiler IR passes, DSATUR register allocation, xv6 RISC-V proportional-share lottery scheduling, copy-on-write virtual memory), database engines (PostgreSQL TPC-H SF 0.1 join ordering and knapsack index selection), quantum algorithms (Grover search, Deutsch-Jozsa, Bernstein-Vazirani, QFT, QPE, Shor order finding, QML vs. classical SVM), and automated software engineering (pugixml test-suite 0-1 set cover minimization) were designed, implemented from first principles in C++17 and Python, and empirically verified against strict mathematical invariants. Every performance claim, speedup ratio, and trade-off documented herein is grounded strictly in concrete empirical measurements logged in repository CSV/JSON files, with simulated and theoretical models explicitly distinguished from physical hardware executions.

Track Report: Track A — Continuous Optimization

Author / AI Pair: Antigravity (Gemini 3.8 Flash)
Track: A_continuous
Evaluation Date: 2026-10-23
Status: Measured on Physical Hardware (C++17, GCC -O3)

1. Objective & Problem Formulation

The goal of Track A is to investigate the performance, convergence rates, hyperparameter sensitivity, and noise resilience of first-order, second-order, and curvature-based continuous optimization algorithms across diverse loss topologies.

Mathematical Formulation

The optimization problem is unconstrained loss minimization:

min⁡θ∈Rdf(θ)\min_{\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d} f(\theta)θ∈Rdmin​f(θ)

Six distinct mathematical landscapes were implemented and benchmarked:

  1. Convex Quadratic (Well-conditioned):
    f1(x,y)=12(x2+2y2),κ=λmax⁡λmin⁡=2.0f_1(x, y) = \frac{1}{2}(x^2 + 2y^2), \quad \kappa = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}} = 2.0f1​(x,y)=21​(x2+2y2),κ=λmin​λmax​​=2.0
    Global minimum: f1(0,0)=0f_1(0, 0) = 0f1​(0,0)=0.
  2. Strongly Convex Quadratic (Ill-conditioned):
    f2(x,y)=12(x2+100y2),κ=100.0,μ=1.0,L=100.0f_2(x, y) = \frac{1}{2}(x^2 + 100y^2), \quad \kappa = 100.0, \quad \mu = 1.0, \quad L = 100.0f2​(x,y)=21​(x2+100y2),κ=100.0,μ=1.0,L=100.0
    Global minimum: f2(0,0)=0f_2(0, 0) = 0f2​(0,0)=0.
  3. Rosenbrock (Non-Convex Curved Banana Valley):
    f3(x,y)=(1−x)2+100(y−x2)2f_3(x, y) = (1 - x)^2 + 100(y - x^2)^2f3​(x,y)=(1−x)2+100(y−x2)2
    Global minimum: f3(1,1)=0f_3(1, 1) = 0f3​(1,1)=0. Exhibits strong non-linear coordinate coupling.
  4. Saddle Point (Indefinite Curvature):
    f4(x,y)=x2−y2,∇2f4(0,0)=diag(+2,−2)f_4(x, y) = x^2 - y^2, \quad \nabla^2 f_4(0, 0) = \text{diag}(+2, -2)f4​(x,y)=x2−y2,∇2f4​(0,0)=diag(+2,−2)
    Stationary critical point at (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) is an unstable strict saddle point with negative curvature along yyy.
  5. Rastrigin (Highly Multimodal Surface):
    f5(x,y)=20+[x2−10cos⁡(2πx)]+[y2−10cos⁡(2πy)]f_5(x, y) = 20 + [x^2 - 10\cos(2\pi x)] + [y^2 - 10\cos(2\pi y)]f5​(x,y)=20+[x2−10cos(2πx)]+[y2−10cos(2πy)]
    Global minimum at (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) surrounded by a dense regular grid of local minima.
  6. Himmelblau (Multimodal with 4 Equal Minima):
    f6(x,y)=(x2+y−11)2+(x+y2−7)2f_6(x, y) = (x^2 + y - 11)^2 + (x + y^2 - 7)^2f6​(x,y)=(x2+y−11)2+(x+y2−7)2
    Four identical global minima where f6(x,y)=0f_6(x, y) = 0f6​(x,y)=0.

In addition, a Two-Layer MLP (2→4→12 \to 4 \to 12→4→1, 17 total parameters) was trained on a non-linear XOR dataset using hand-written reverse-mode backpropagation without external libraries.

2. Baseline

The baseline for all comparisons is Standard Batch Gradient Descent (GD):

θt+1=θt−η∇f(θt)\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta \nabla f(\theta_t)θt+1​=θt​−η∇f(θt​)
All optimizers were initialized at the exact same starting points (x0x_0x0​), evaluated over the same learning rate grid, and terminated using identical stopping criteria: - Maximum iterations: $500$ - Gradient norm tolerance: ∥∇f(θ)∥<10−5\|\nabla f(\theta)\| < 10^{-5}∥∇f(θ)∥<10−5

5. Visualizations & Figures Referenced

Figure 1: Convergence Curves across Landscape Topologies

  • Panel (a) Convex Quadratic: All algorithms rapidly reach numerical zero; GD reaches 1.64×10−111.64 \times 10^{-11}1.64×10−11 in 20 iterations.
  • Panel (b) Strongly Convex (κ=100\kappa = 100κ=100): Standard GD exhibits extreme horizontal oscillation, stalling at 1.94×10−41.94 \times 10^{-4}1.94×10−4 after 500 iterations. In contrast, NAG and Adam descend monotonically along the valley, achieving loss <10−11< 10^{-11}<10−11 in under 200 iterations.
  • Panel (c) Rosenbrock Valley: GD crawls along the valley floor (f=0.3087f = 0.3087f=0.3087). Adam's coordinate-wise adaptive step sizes navigate the curvature, achieving 3.08×10−53.08 \times 10^{-5}3.08×10−5 at 500 iterations.
  • Panel (d) Saddle Point (x2−y2x^2 - y^2x2−y2): Demonstrates unbounded descent along the negative eigenvalue direction towards −∞-\infty−∞. Momentum accelerates divergence (1028310^{283}10283 within 500 steps), whereas AdaGrad's cumulative sum-of-squares gracefully dampens the step sizes, containing descent to −979.66-979.66−979.66.

Figure 2: Learning Rate Sensitivity Grid

  • Illustrates the stability boundary for GD: learning rates η≥0.05\eta \ge 0.05η≥0.05 on the κ=100\kappa = 100κ=100 quadratic lead to catastrophic divergence (f→∞f \to \inftyf→∞).
  • Adaptive methods (RMSProp, Adam) tolerate a substantially broader range of η∈[0.01,0.5]\eta \in [0.01, 0.5]η∈[0.01,0.5] without divergence.

Figure 3: Noise Resilience Comparison

  • Compares the empirical Mean ±\pm± Standard Deviation across 10 stochastic seeds.
  • On Rosenbrock, GD exhibits high variance (0.712±0.2660.712 \pm 0.2660.712±0.266), whereas Momentum (0.0018±0.00010.0018 \pm 0.00010.0018±0.0001) and Adam (0.00007±0.000070.00007 \pm 0.000070.00007±0.00007) exhibit remarkable stability under noisy gradient evaluations.

6. Trade-offs and Honest Limitations

  1. Ill-Conditioned Ravines (κ=100\kappa = 100κ=100):
    • Data Evidence: GD required η≤0.01\eta \le 0.01η≤0.01 and failed to converge within 500 iterations (loss $0.00019$).
    • Limitation: First-order GD cannot adapt to anisotropic curvature. Second-order Newton's method completely solves this, reaching (0,0)(0, 0)(0,0) in exactly 1 step with loss <10−14< 10^{-14}<10−14, but requires computing and inverting an explicit O(d2)O(d^2)O(d2) Hessian matrix.
  2. AdaGrad Diminishing Learning Rate Trap:
    • Data Evidence: On Rosenbrock, AdaGrad achieved a poor final loss of $0.7800$ (worse than baseline GD's best run).
    • Root Cause: AdaGrad's accumulator Gt=Gt−1+gt2G_t = G_{t-1} + g_t^2Gt​=Gt−1​+gt2​ is monotonically non-decreasing. In long curved valleys requiring many iterations, the effective learning rate ηGt\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{G_t}}Gt​​η​ shrinks to near zero prematurely, freezing progress before reaching the minimum.
    • Solution: RMSProp and Adam replace the monotonic accumulator with an exponential moving average (1−β)(1 - \beta)(1−β), preventing step size death.
  3. Saddle Point Behavior (x2−y2x^2 - y^2x2−y2):
    • Data Evidence: All algorithms descend along yyy towards −∞-\infty−∞.
    • Honest Clarification: In unconstrained continuous optimization, saddle points with negative eigenvalues are not local minima; gradient descent naturally escapes along negative curvature directions. When escaping saddles, Momentum accelerates escape dramatically, whereas AdaGrad bounds the velocity.
  4. Local Minima Trapping on Multimodal Landscapes (Rastrigin):
    • Data Evidence: NAG (η=0.001\eta=0.001η=0.001), AdaGrad (η=0.25\eta=0.25η=0.25), and RMSProp (η=0.05\eta=0.05η=0.05) all terminated in identical local minima (f=7.95966f = 7.95966f=7.95966), while Adam reached a lower local minimum (f=1.98992f = 1.98992f=1.98992).
    • Limitation: No deterministic gradient method guarantees finding the global minimum on multimodal surfaces without global exploration or restart strategies.
  5. Noisy Gradient Degradation on RMSProp:
    • Data Evidence: On the ill-conditioned quadratic, clean RMSProp reached 4.32×10−154.32 \times 10^{-15}4.32×10−15, but under noise σ=0.05\sigma = 0.05σ=0.05 degraded to loss 3.151±0.0673.151 \pm 0.0673.151±0.067.
    • Root Cause: RMSProp lacks first-moment momentum filtering; high-frequency gradient noise directly perturbs the parameter step. In contrast, Adam combines first-moment averaging (mtm_tmt​) with second moments (vtv_tvt​), maintaining a noisy loss of 0.00096±0.001030.00096 \pm 0.001030.00096±0.00103.

Section 2

Track Report: B_discrete (Discrete, Combinatorial & QUBO Optimization)

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Combinatorial optimization in discrete decision spaces, encompassing resource allocation (0/1 Knapsack), graph clustering (Max-Cut), and subset selection (mRMR Feature Selection).
  • Observed Bottleneck / Inefficiency: Discrete optimization problems are NP-hard. Classical heuristics (greedy) execute in near-instantaneous O(Nlog⁡N)O(N \log N)O(NlogN) time but frequently get trapped in suboptimal local extrema due to myopic decision-making. Conversely, naive brute-force exhaustive search exhibits O(2N)O(2^N)O(2N) exponential complexity, becoming intractable beyond N≈30N \approx 30N≈30.
  • Baseline Description:
    • Knapsack Baseline: Dantzig value-to-weight ratio greedy heuristic (ratio=vi/wi\text{ratio} = v_i / w_iratio=vi​/wi​).
    • Max-Cut Baseline: Node-by-node greedy cut expansion (Sahni & Gonzalez, 1976) guaranteeing at least a $0.5$ approximation ratio.
    • Feature Selection Baseline: Forward greedy selection picking features step-wise based on instantaneous marginal gain.

2. Mathematical Formulations

2.1 0/1 Knapsack Problem (ILP & Dynamic Programming)

Given NNN items with values vi>0v_i > 0vi​>0, weights wi>0w_i > 0wi​>0, and knapsack capacity W>0W > 0W>0:

max⁡x∈{0,1}N∑i=1Nvixisubject to∑i=1Nwixi≤W\max_{x \in \{0, 1\}^N} \sum_{i=1}^N v_i x_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i=1}^N w_i x_i \le Wx∈{0,1}Nmax​i=1∑N​vi​xi​subject toi=1∑N​wi​xi​≤W
  • Dynamic Programming Formulation:
    DP(i,w)=max⁡(DP(i−1,w), DP(i−1,w−wi)+vi)for w≥wiDP(i, w) = \max\left(DP(i-1, w), \, DP(i-1, w - w_i) + v_i\right) \quad \text{for } w \ge w_iDP(i,w)=max(DP(i−1,w),DP(i−1,w−wi​)+vi​)for w≥wi​
    with base case DP(0,w)=0DP(0, w) = 0DP(0,w)=0. Complexity: O(N⋅W)O(N \cdot W)O(N⋅W) pseudo-polynomial time and space.
  • Branch-and-Bound Formulation: Best-first search using Dantzig's fractional LP relaxation upper bound:
    Bound(level,cur_val,cur_wt)=cur_val+∑j∈fitvj+W−wtitem_wt⋅item_val\text{Bound}(\text{level}, \text{cur\_val}, \text{cur\_wt}) = \text{cur\_val} + \sum_{j \in \text{fit}} v_j + \frac{W - \text{wt}}{\text{item\_wt}} \cdot \text{item\_val}Bound(level,cur_val,cur_wt)=cur_val+j∈fit∑​vj​+item_wtW−wt​⋅item_val

2.2 Knapsack Encoded as QUBO with Penalty Terms

To convert inequality constraints ∑i=1Nwixi≤W\sum_{i=1}^N w_i x_i \le W∑i=1N​wi​xi​≤W into an unconstrained QUBO, K=⌊log⁡2W⌋+1K = \lfloor \log_2 W \rfloor + 1K=⌊log2​W⌋+1 binary slack variables sk∈{0,1}s_k \in {0, 1}sk​∈{0,1} are introduced:

∑i=1Nwixi+∑k=0K−12ksk=W\sum_{i=1}^N w_i x_i + \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} 2^k s_k = Wi=1∑N​wi​xi​+k=0∑K−1​2ksk​=W
The quadratic unconstrained minimization objective is formulated as:
min⁡x,s∈{0,1}H(x,s)=−∑i=1Nvixi+P(∑i=1Nwixi+∑k=0K−12ksk−W)2\min_{x, s \in \{0, 1\}} H(x, s) = -\sum_{i=1}^N v_i x_i + P \left(\sum_{i=1}^N w_i x_i + \sum_{k=0}^{K-1} 2^k s_k - W\right)^2x,s∈{0,1}min​H(x,s)=−i=1∑N​vi​xi​+P(i=1∑N​wi​xi​+k=0∑K−1​2ksk​−W)2
where penalty scalar P>max⁡iviP > \max_i v_iP>maxi​vi​ ensures any constraint violation incurs an energy penalty exceeding any objective gain.

2.3 Max-Cut and Explicit Binary-to-Spin QUBO/Ising Conversion

For an undirected graph G=(V,E)G = (V, E)G=(V,E) with edge weights wuv>0w_{uv} > 0wuv​>0:

Cut(x)=∑(u,v)∈Ewuv[xu(1−xv)+xv(1−xu)]\text{Cut}(x) = \sum_{(u, v) \in E} w_{uv} \left[ x_u (1 - x_v) + x_v (1 - x_u) \right]Cut(x)=(u,v)∈E∑​wuv​[xu​(1−xv​)+xv​(1−xu​)]
  • QUBO Matrix Formulation:
    min⁡x∈{0,1}nHQUBO(x)=xTQx=−Cut(x)\min_{x \in \{0, 1\}^n} H_{\text{QUBO}}(x) = x^T Q x = -\text{Cut}(x)x∈{0,1}nmin​HQUBO​(x)=xTQx=−Cut(x)
    where:
    Quu=−∑(u,v)∈Ewuv,Quv=2wuv(u<v)Q_{uu} = -\sum_{(u, v) \in E} w_{uv}, \qquad Q_{uv} = 2 w_{uv} \quad (u < v)Quu​=−(u,v)∈E∑​wuv​,Quv​=2wuv​(u<v)
  • Explicit Binary-to-Spin Conversion: Substituting xi=1+σi2x_i = \frac{1 + \sigma_i}{2}xi​=21+σi​​ with σi∈{−1,+1}\sigma_i \in {-1, +1}σi​∈{−1,+1} yields:
    xu(1−xv)+xv(1−xu)=1−σuσv2x_u (1 - x_v) + x_v (1 - x_u) = \frac{1 - \sigma_u \sigma_v}{2}xu​(1−xv​)+xv​(1−xu​)=21−σu​σv​​
    Summing across all edges produces the Ising Hamiltonian:
    HIsing(σ)=12∑(u,v)∈Ewuvσuσv−12∑(u,v)∈EwuvH_{\text{Ising}}(\sigma) = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(u, v) \in E} w_{uv} \sigma_u \sigma_v - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{(u, v) \in E} w_{uv}HIsing​(σ)=21​(u,v)∈E∑​wuv​σu​σv​−21​(u,v)∈E∑​wuv​
    Exact algebraic identity HQUBO(x)≡HIsing(σ)H_{\text{QUBO}}(x) \equiv H_{\text{Ising}}(\sigma)HQUBO​(x)≡HIsing​(σ) holds for every binary configuration x∈{0,1}nx \in \{0, 1\}^nx∈{0,1}n and corresponding spin configuration σ∈{−1,+1}n\sigma \in \{-1, +1\}^nσ∈{−1,+1}n.

Selecting kkk of nnn features balancing relevance reli\text{rel}ireli​ and redundancy redij\text{red}{ij}redij​:

min⁡x∈{0,1}nHFS(x)=−α∑i=1nrelixi+β∑i<jredijxixj+P(∑i=1nxi−k)2\min_{x \in \{0, 1\}^n} H_{\text{FS}}(x) = -\alpha \sum_{i=1}^n \text{rel}_i x_i + \beta \sum_{i < j} \text{red}_{ij} x_i x_j + P \left(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i - k\right)^2x∈{0,1}nmin​HFS​(x)=−αi=1∑n​reli​xi​+βi<j∑​redij​xi​xj​+P(i=1∑n​xi​−k)2
Expanding the cardinality penalty P(∑xi−k)2P (\sum x_i - k)^2P(∑xi​−k)2:
P(∑i=1nxi2+2∑i<jxixj−2k∑i=1nxi+k2)=P(1−2k)∑i=1nxi+2P∑i<jxixj+Pk2P \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2 + 2 \sum_{i < j} x_i x_j - 2k \sum_{i=1}^n x_i + k^2 \right) = P(1 - 2k) \sum_{i=1}^n x_i + 2P \sum_{i < j} x_i x_j + P k^2P(i=1∑n​xi2​+2i<j∑​xi​xj​−2ki=1∑n​xi​+k2)=P(1−2k)i=1∑n​xi​+2Pi<j∑​xi​xj​+Pk2
This maps cleanly into diagonal and off-diagonal elements of QQQ.

3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

  • Chosen Methods:
    1. Greedy Heuristics: O(Nlog⁡N)O(N \log N)O(NlogN) sorting baseline.
    2. Dynamic Programming: Guaranteed pseudo-polynomial O(N⋅W)O(N \cdot W)O(N⋅W) global optimum.
    3. Branch-and-Bound (B&B): Tree search with Dantzig fractional LP relaxation bounding.
    4. Integer Linear Programming (ILP): Google OR-Tools with SCIP/CBC branch-and-cut backend.
    5. Simulated Annealing on QUBO: Metropolis-Hastings Markov chain search over energy landscape.
  • Why Suitable: Directly maps the continuous-to-discrete optimization progression described in Chapter 6: exact relaxation bounds (fractional LP), penalty formulations for constraint handling, and Hamiltonian mapping for combinatorial landscapes.

4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

  • Environment: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on WSL2 / x86_64, GCC 13.3.0 (-O3 -std=c++17).
  • Timing Measurement: Monotonic hardware timers via std::chrono::steady_clock reporting microsecond (μs\mu\text{s}μs) latency.
  • Deterministic Seeds: Fixed seed 42 for random instance generation; seeds 201..210 for 10 stochastic simulated annealing runs.
  • Fair Comparison: Identical problem instances, exact same capacities WWW, and identical stopping tolerances.
  • Correctness Check: DP, B&B, and ILP verified to produce identical values down to 10−510^{-5}10−5 tolerance across all problem sizes.

6. Analysis, Trade-offs & Limitations

6.1 Where Greedy Fails

  1. Knapsack Granularity Mismatch: Greedy packs items in decreasing order of vi/wiv_i/w_ivi​/wi​. If the last item doesn't fit, greedy stops, leaving dead capacity that could have accommodated lower-ratio items with higher combined value. This caused a 6.37% gap at N=10N=10N=10 and a 0.41% gap at N=100N=100N=100.
  2. Feature Selection Submodular Interference: In mRMR, greedy commits irrevocably to the highest individual relevance feature. However, if that feature has high pairwise redundancy with remaining high-value features, the entire subsequent set is corrupted (resulting in the observed $0.90$ vs. $1.70$ failure).

6.2 Where Branch-and-Bound and Dynamic Programming Diverge

  1. Pseudo-polynomial Growth of DP: DP runtime is strictly proportional to N⋅WN \cdot WN⋅W. At N=500,W=6944N=500, W=6944N=500,W=6944, DP required allocating a 501×6945501 \times 6945501×6945 table (3.48×1063.48 \times 10^63.48×106 entries), consuming 116.28 ms116.28\text{ ms}116.28 ms. If WWW were scaled to 10710^7107 or if weights were non-integer floats, DP would exhaust memory.
  2. Pruning Power of Dantzig's LP Bound: On uncorrelated random knapsack instances, the fractional relaxation upper bound is exceptionally tight (Δ≤max⁡ivi\Delta \le \max_i v_iΔ≤maxi​vi​). As a result, B&B pruned nearly the entire tree, solving N=500N=500N=500 in 5.38 ms5.38\text{ ms}5.38 ms—21.6×21.6\times21.6× faster than DP and 5.8×5.8\times5.8× faster than OR-Tools ILP (31.12 ms31.12\text{ ms}31.12 ms).
  3. Where B&B Blows Up (Theoretical Limitation): When instances are strongly correlated (vi=wi+cv_i = w_i + cvi​=wi​+c), the fractional upper bound matches the integral value across numerous branches, causing B&B to degrade toward worst-case O(2N)O(2^N)O(2N) tree enumeration.

6.3 QUBO Penalty Limitations

  1. Penalty Tuning Vulnerability: Encoding constraints like ∑wixi=W\sum w_i x_i = W∑wi​xi​=W requires quadratic penalties P(∑wixi−W)2P (\sum w_i x_i - W)^2P(∑wi​xi​−W)2. If PPP is chosen too small, the solver accepts infeasible constraint violations; if PPP is chosen too large, the energy eigenvalues of the penalty dwarf the objective, flattening the solution space and stalling classical simulated annealing or quantum QAOA.
  2. Slack Variable Overhead: Representing an integer capacity WWW requires ∼log⁡2W\sim \log_2 W∼log2​W auxiliary slack qubits, increasing the qubit register size from NNN to N+⌈log⁡2W⌉N + \lceil\log_2 W\rceilN+⌈log2​W⌉.

6.4 Status Categorization

  • Knapsack Runtimes & Values: Measured on hardware (WSL Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, std::chrono::steady_clock).
  • Exact Equivalence (DP == B&B == ILP): Formally measured and verified on identical instances.
  • Max-Cut & Feature Selection Annealing: Simulated classically via Metropolis-Hastings Markov chains (10 seeds, Mean ±\pm± Std).

Section 3

Track Report: C_quantum (Quantum Optimization: QAOA, VQE, QNN & Annealing Limits)

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Variational quantum algorithms (VQA) and hybrid quantum-classical optimization applied to combinatorial optimization (QAOA for Max-Cut), quantum chemistry / condensed matter physics (VQE for molecular H2H_2H2​ and Transverse-Field Ising Models), and quantum machine learning (PQC classifiers).
  • Observed Bottlenecks & Inefficiencies:
    1. Barren Plateaus: In parameterized quantum circuits forming approximate Haar 2-designs, the gradient variance of global cost functions vanishes exponentially with the qubit count (Var∼2−n\text{Var} \sim 2^{-n}Var∼2−n), rendering gradient descent intractable on deep architectures.
    2. Quantum Projection (Shot) Noise: On physical hardware, statevector amplitudes are inaccessible; observables must be estimated from finite measurement shots SSS, introducing statistical variance scaling as O(1/S)\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{S})O(1/S​).
    3. Hardware Noise & Decoherence: Real NISQ devices suffer from gate infidelities (0.1%0.1%0.1% single-qubit, 1%1%1% two-qubit) and state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) readout errors (1–2%1\text{--}2%1–2%), which bias energy estimates and degrade quantum entanglement.
    4. Quantum Annealing Embedding Bottlenecks: Physical quantum annealers have sparse connectivity graphs (Chimera, Pegasus), requiring minor embedding with physical qubit chains, chain breaks, and severe dynamic range compression.
  • Baseline Description:
    • QAOA: Compared against brute-force global optimum cut ($15.0$) from Track B.
    • VQE: Compared against exact classical matrix diagonalization (numpy.linalg.eigh).
    • Quantum Gradients: Classical parameter-shift Euclidean baseline vs. stochastic SPSA vs. Riemannian Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG).

2. Mathematical Formulations

2.1 Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA)

For a graph G=(V,E)G = (V, E)G=(V,E) with Max-Cut Ising Hamiltonian HC=∑(u,v)∈EJuvZuZv+offset⋅IH_C = \sum_{(u,v) \in E} J_{uv} Z_u Z_v + \text{offset} \cdot IHC​=∑(u,v)∈E​Juv​Zu​Zv​+offset⋅I, the ppp-layer variational state is:

∣ψ(γ⃗,β⃗)⟩=∏l=1p(e−iβlHBe−iγlHC)∣+⟩⊗n|\psi(\vec{\gamma}, \vec{\beta})\rangle = \prod_{l=1}^p \left( e^{-i \beta_l H_B} e^{-i \gamma_l H_C} \right) |+\rangle^{\otimes n}∣ψ(γ​,β​)⟩=l=1∏p​(e−iβl​HB​e−iγl​HC​)∣+⟩⊗n
where HB=∑j=1nXjH_B = \sum_{j=1}^n X_jHB​=∑j=1n​Xj​ is the transverse mixer Hamiltonian. The expected cut is maximized by minimizing:
⟨HC(γ⃗,β⃗)⟩=⟨ψ(γ⃗,β⃗)∣HC∣ψ(γ⃗,β⃗)⟩,⟨Cut⟩=−⟨HC⟩\langle H_C(\vec{\gamma}, \vec{\beta}) \rangle = \langle \psi(\vec{\gamma}, \vec{\beta}) | H_C | \psi(\vec{\gamma}, \vec{\beta}) \rangle, \qquad \langle \text{Cut} \rangle = -\langle H_C \rangle⟨HC​(γ​,β​)⟩=⟨ψ(γ​,β​)∣HC​∣ψ(γ​,β​)⟩,⟨Cut⟩=−⟨HC​⟩
The approximation ratio is defined as α=⟨Cut⟩Cut∗\alpha = \frac{\langle \text{Cut} \rangle}{\text{Cut}^*}α=Cut∗⟨Cut⟩​.

2.2 Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)

VQE exploits the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle to estimate the ground state energy E0E_0E0​:

E0≤min⁡θ⃗⟨H⟩θ⃗=⟨ψ(θ⃗)∣H∣ψ(θ⃗)⟩E_0 \le \min_{\vec{\theta}} \langle H \rangle_{\vec{\theta}} = \langle \psi(\vec{\theta}) | H | \psi(\vec{\theta}) \rangleE0​≤θmin​⟨H⟩θ​=⟨ψ(θ)∣H∣ψ(θ)⟩
- **Molecular H2H_2H2​ Hamiltonian** (R=0.735 A˚R = 0.735\text{ \AA}R=0.735 A˚, STO-3G parity reduction):
HH2=−1.052373II+0.397937ZI−0.397937IZ−0.011280ZZ+0.180931XXH_{H_2} = -1.052373 II + 0.397937 ZI - 0.397937 IZ - 0.011280 ZZ + 0.180931 XXHH2​​=−1.052373II+0.397937ZI−0.397937IZ−0.011280ZZ+0.180931XX
- **2-Qubit Transverse-Field Ising Model (TFIM)** (J=1.0,g=0.8J=1.0, g=0.8J=1.0,g=0.8):
HTFIM=−1.0ZZ−0.8IX−0.8XIH_{\text{TFIM}} = -1.0 ZZ - 0.8 IX - 0.8 XIHTFIM​=−1.0ZZ−0.8IX−0.8XI

2.3 Quantum Gradient Estimation Methods

  1. Parameter-Shift Rule (PSR): For gates generated by Pauli generators G=e−iθ2PG = e^{-i \frac{\theta}{2} P}G=e−i2θ​P, the exact analytical gradient is:
    ∂⟨H⟩∂θk=⟨H⟩θk+π2−⟨H⟩θk−π22\frac{\partial \langle H \rangle}{\partial \theta_k} = \frac{\langle H \rangle_{\theta_k + \frac{\pi}{2}} - \langle H \rangle_{\theta_k - \frac{\pi}{2}}}{2}∂θk​∂⟨H⟩​=2⟨H⟩θk​+2π​​−⟨H⟩θk​−2π​​​
    Requires 2D2D2D circuit evaluations per gradient step (DDD parameters).
  2. Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (SPSA): Random Bernoulli perturbation Δ∈{−1,+1}D\Delta \in {-1, +1}^DΔ∈{−1,+1}D:
    gk=L(θ+ctΔ)−L(θ−ctΔ)2ctΔkg_k = \frac{\mathcal{L}(\theta + c_t \Delta) - \mathcal{L}(\theta - c_t \Delta)}{2 c_t \Delta_k}gk​=2ct​Δk​L(θ+ct​Δ)−L(θ−ct​Δ)​
    Requires exactly $2$ circuit evaluations per step, independent of parameter dimension DDD.
  3. Quantum Natural Gradient (QNG): Preconditions the Euclidean gradient with the Fubini-Study metric tensor FFF:
    Fkl(θ⃗)=Re[⟨∂kψ∣∂lψ⟩−⟨∂kψ∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣∂lψ⟩]F_{kl}(\vec{\theta}) = \text{Re} \left[ \langle \partial_k \psi | \partial_l \psi \rangle - \langle \partial_k \psi | \psi \rangle \langle \psi | \partial_l \psi \rangle \right]Fkl​(θ)=Re[⟨∂k​ψ∣∂l​ψ⟩−⟨∂k​ψ∣ψ⟩⟨ψ∣∂l​ψ⟩]
    Update rule: θ⃗t+1=θ⃗t−η(F+ϵI)−1∇L(θ⃗t)\vec{\theta}_{t+1} = \vec{\theta}_t - \eta (F + \epsilon I)^{-1} \nabla \mathcal{L}(\vec{\theta}_t)θt+1​=θt​−η(F+ϵI)−1∇L(θt​).

2.4 Barren Plateaus Scaling

For an ensemble of circuits forming an approximate 2-design over the unitary group U(2n)U(2^n)U(2n):

Varθ⃗[∂⟨Hglobal⟩∂θk]∈O(12n)\text{Var}_{\vec{\theta}} \left[ \frac{\partial \langle H_{\text{global}} \rangle}{\partial \theta_k} \right] \in \mathcal{O}\left( \frac{1}{2^n} \right)Varθ​[∂θk​∂⟨Hglobal​⟩​]∈O(2n1​)
when Hglobal=Z⊗nH_{\text{global}} = Z^{\otimes n}Hglobal​=Z⊗n, whereas local observables Hlocal=Z0H_{\text{local}} = Z_0Hlocal​=Z0​ preserve polynomial gradient variance O(1/poly(n))\mathcal{O}(1/\text{poly}(n))O(1/poly(n)).

3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

  • Chosen Methods:
    1. QAOA (p=1,2,3p=1, 2, 3p=1,2,3): Maps discrete combinatorial Max-Cut into continuous unitary rotation angles.
    2. VQE with RealAmplitudes Ansatz: Hybrid quantum-classical optimization combining RY–CNOTRY\text{--}\text{CNOT}RY–CNOT layers with BFGS, COBYLA, and SLSQP.
    3. QNG Optimizer: Riemannian natural gradient descent accounting for quantum state manifold curvature.
    4. Aer Noise Simulator: Hardware-calibrated thermal/depolarizing and readout noise models.
  • Why Suitable: Directly realizes Chapter 6 concepts: continuous relaxations of discrete spaces, non-convex variational landscapes, geometric optimization on Riemannian manifolds, and noise sensitivity in physical computing.

4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

  • Simulation Environment: Ubuntu 24.04 on WSL2 / x86_64, Python 3.12, Qiskit 2.6.1, Qiskit Aer 0.18.0, SciPy 1.18.1.
  • Deterministic Evaluation: Fixed random seeds (seeds 100..109 for QAOA, VQE, QNN; seeds 500..509 for shots; seeds 601..610 for noise; seeds 702..710 for barren plateaus).
  • Stopping Criteria: Uniform optimization tolerance 10−710^{-7}10−7 for VQE, 10−410^{-4}10−4 for QAOA; 35 iterations for QNN.
  • Exact Benchmarks: Classical brute-force Max-Cut ($15.0$) from Track B JSON; full matrix exact diagonalization (eigh) for H2H_2H2​ and TFIM.

6. Limits of Embedding QUBO on Quantum Annealing Hardware

While gate-based QPUs execute parameterized unitary transformations, quantum annealers (e.g., D-Wave Advantage and 2000Q) minimize classical Ising spin Hamiltonians by adiabatically evolving a transverse-field driver into a target problem Hamiltonian:

H(s)=−(1−s)∑iΔiXi+s[∑ihiZi+∑(i,j)JijZiZj]H(s) = -(1 - s) \sum_i \Delta_i X_i + s \left[ \sum_i h_i Z_i + \sum_{(i, j)} J_{ij} Z_i Z_j \right]H(s)=−(1−s)i∑​Δi​Xi​+s​i∑​hi​Zi​+(i,j)∑​Jij​Zi​Zj​​

Embedding real-world QUBO problems onto physical annealing hardware faces severe physical and mathematical limitations:

6.1 Sparse Physical Topology vs. Dense Problem Graphs

  • Graph Degree Mismatch: Physical QPUs have limited connectivity. D-Wave Chimera graphs have qubit degree 6 (bipartite K4,4K_{4,4}K4,4​ cells); the newer Pegasus topology has degree 15; Zephyr topology has degree 20.
  • Clique Embedding (KnK_nKn​) Explosion: Combinatorial optimization problems (e.g., dense Max-Cut, TSP, or knapsack with quadratic penalties ∑wixi\sum w_i x_i∑wi​xi​) require dense all-to-all quadratic couplings KnK_nKn​.
  • Embedding an nnn-node complete graph onto a sparse physical grid requires minor embedding, where a single logical variable is mapped to a connected chain of physical qubits. On Chimera graphs, embedding KnK_nKn​ requires O(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^2)O(n2) physical qubits. For example, embedding a fully connected graph of just N=64N=64N=64 logical variables consumes over 1,000 physical qubits.

6.2 Ferromagnetic Coupling, Chain Breaks, and Energy Distortion

  • To force physical qubits in chain CuC_uCu​ to behave as a single logical spin sus_usu​, strong ferromagnetic couplings −JchainZiZj-J_{\text{chain}} Z_i Z_j−Jchain​Zi​Zj​ (Jchain>0J_{\text{chain}} > 0Jchain​>0) are applied between adjacent physical qubits in the chain.
  • Dynamic Range Compression: Hardware couplers operate within a bounded physical range (typically J∈[−1.0,+1.0]J \in [-1.0, +1.0]J∈[−1.0,+1.0] and h∈[−2.0,+2.0]h \in [-2.0, +2.0]h∈[−2.0,+2.0]). Setting Jchain≥2max⁡∣Juv∣J_{\text{chain}} \ge 2 \max |J_{uv}|Jchain​≥2max∣Juv​∣ forces all logical problem couplings JuvJ_{uv}Juv​ to be scaled down by a factor of 1/Jchain1 / J_{\text{chain}}1/Jchain​.
  • Loss of Energy Resolution: Scaling down the logical Hamiltonian compresses the energy gap ΔE\Delta EΔE between the ground state and excited states. The compressed energy differences frequently fall below the analog control error (ICE) and thermal noise threshold (kBT≈12–15 mK≈1 GHzk_B T \approx 12\text{--}15\text{ mK} \approx 1\text{ GHz}kB​T≈12–15 mK≈1 GHz), destroying ground-state fidelity.
  • Chain Breaks: When thermal fluctuations or non-adiabatic transitions overcome JchainJ_{\text{chain}}Jchain​, physical qubits within the same logical chain disagree (e.g., some read +1+1+1, others −1-1−1). Resolving chain breaks requires classical heuristics (e.g., majority voting or weighted averaging), which introduces post-processing bias and voids global optimality guarantees.

6.3 Analog Control Precision and Precision Noise

  • Unlike digital gate-based quantum circuits, quantum annealers specify coupler biases via digital-to-analog converters (DACs) with only 4–54\text{--}54–5 bits of effective resolution (quantization error ∼2–3%\sim 2\text{--}3%∼2–3%).
  • Minor-embedded Hamiltonians with delicate penalty terms (such as knapsack capacity penalties P(∑wixi−W)2P(\sum w_i x_i - W)^2P(∑wi​xi​−W)2) become severely distorted by DAC quantization and 1/f1/f1/f flux noise, leading the physical annealer to return infeasible bitstrings that violate constraints.

Section 4

Track Report: D_submodular_parallel (Submodular, Parallel, Federated & Multi-Task Optimization)

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Discrete submodular maximization, shared-memory multicore parallelism, decentralized federated learning, and multi-task gradient balancing.
  • Observed Bottlenecks & Inefficiencies:
    1. Submodular Optimization: Exact maximum coverage is NP-hard. Brute-force combinatorial search (nk)\binom{n}{k}(kn​) scales factorially, becoming intractable beyond n≈25n \approx 25n≈25.
    2. Multicore Scaling Overhead: Synchronization barriers, thread pool dispatch latency, atomic queue contention, and hardware core oversubscription limit parallel scaling and break Amdahl's law when task granularity is too fine.
    3. Federated Client Drift: When data is heterogeneous (Non-IID label skew), performing many local SGD steps (EEE) causes local client parameters to drift toward local empirical minimizers, degrading global model aggregation.
    4. Multi-Task Gradient Conflict: Competing tasks with conflicting gradients (g1Tg2<0g_1^T g_2 < 0g1T​g2​<0) cause destructive interference under uniform equal weighting, while naive Pareto optimization can stall shared feature learning prematurely.
  • Baseline Descriptions:
    • Max-Coverage: Compared against exact combinatorial brute-force optimum f(A∗)f(A^*)f(A∗) and the theoretical (1−1/e)(1 - 1/e)(1−1/e) lower bound.
    • Parallel Workload: Compared against single-threaded serial execution time (Tserial=568.60 msT_{\text{serial}} = 568.60\text{ ms}Tserial​=568.60 ms).
    • Federated Learning: Compared against centralized batch SGD (N=1,500N=1,500N=1,500 samples, $500$ steps).
    • Multi-Task Optimization: Compared against static equal weighting (Ltotal=0.5L1+0.5L2\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = 0.5 \mathcal{L}_1 + 0.5 \mathcal{L}_2Ltotal​=0.5L1​+0.5L2​).

2. Mathematical Formulations

3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

  • Chosen Methods:
    1. Greedy Set Coverage: Demonstrates submodular greedy heuristics with provable approximation ratios.
    2. Parallel Frameworks: OpenMP static/dynamic vs. std::thread static/dynamic/work-stealing.
    3. FedAvg: Distributed asynchronous-to-synchronous gradient aggregation under communication constraints.
    4. Multi-Task Balancing: Pareto-stationary multi-objective optimization (MGDA) and adaptive gradient re-weighting (GradNorm).
  • Why Suitable: Directly maps Chapter 6 principles: submodular structure in combinatorial spaces, parallel scalability bounds, decentralized consensus optimization, and Pareto frontier navigation.

4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

  • Hardware & Environment: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on WSL2 / x86_64, GCC 13.3.0 (-O3 -fopenmp -std=c++17).
  • Timing Measurement: Monotonic hardware timers via std::chrono::steady_clock reporting millisecond and microsecond resolution.
  • Deterministic Evaluation: Fixed random seeds (seeds 101..402 for max-coverage, seed 42 for parallel Monte Carlo, seeds 100..109 for FedAvg and multi-task runs).
  • Fair Baseline Parity: Identical total path counts for parallel workloads (2×1062 \times 10^62×106 paths), identical dataset samples (N=1,500N=1,500N=1,500 train, N=500N=500N=500 test for FedAvg; N=500N=500N=500 for MTL), and identical learning rates.

6. Analysis, Trade-offs & Honest Limitations

6.1 Submodularity Trade-offs

  • Where Greedy Excels: On uniform unit-cost cardinality constraints (∣A∣≤k|A| \le k∣A∣≤k), greedy achieved near-optimal coverage ($0.9310$ to $1.0000$), far exceeding the (1−1/e)≈0.632(1 - 1/e) \approx 0.632(1−1/e)≈0.632 worst-case bound.
  • Where Greedy Fails (Honest Limitation): If subsets have non-uniform costs cic_ici​, greedy by marginal gain Δ(e∣A)\Delta(e \mid A)Δ(e∣A) can perform arbitrarily poorly (yielding an unbounded approximation ratio). Even greedy by cost-effectiveness Δ(e∣A)/ci\Delta(e \mid A) / c_iΔ(e∣A)/ci​ fails unless blended with partial enumeration (Khuller et al., 1999).

6.2 Multicore Scalability & Hardware Bottlenecks

  • Core Oversubscription: OpenMP Static reached near-linear speedup at 4 cores (3.81×3.81\times3.81×, 95%95%95% efficiency), closely matching Amdahl's prediction (3.62×3.62\times3.62×). However, scaling collapsed at 8 threads (S=3.35×,E=0.42S=3.35\times, E=0.42S=3.35×,E=0.42) because WSL was provisioned with 4 virtual cores, causing hyperthread contention and thread preemption.
  • Task Granularity Breakdown: For coarse-grained chunks ($50,000$ paths), atomic dispatch overhead was negligible (154.6 ms154.6\text{ ms}154.6 ms). Reducing chunk size to $50$ paths triggered severe mutex contention and cache bouncing, causing a 2.43×2.43\times2.43× latency penalty (375.3 ms375.3\text{ ms}375.3 ms).

6.3 Federated Learning Dynamics

  • Communication Savings: FedAvg with E=20,R=25E=20, R=25E=20,R=25 converged to the exact centralized baseline loss ($0.4217$) and accuracy (80.00%80.00%80.00%), transferring only $20,000$ bytes compared to the gigabytes required to centralize raw data.
  • Non-IID Client Drift: Under label skew, client updates initially pulled local models toward divergent class boundaries. Frequent global communication (R≥25R \ge 25R≥25) was necessary to prevent persistent parameter divergence.

6.4 Honest Multi-Task Evaluation (Why GradNorm Outperformed MGDA)

  • GradNorm Superiority: GradNorm dynamically re-weighted loss gradients according to relative inverse training rates (riαr_i^\alphariα​), achieving the lowest Task 1 Loss ($0.1590$), lowest Task 2 Loss ($0.3069$), and fastest runtime (55.81 ms55.81\text{ ms}55.81 ms).
  • The Pitfall of MGDA (Honest Conclusion): While MGDA guarantees Pareto stationarity, in deep/shared neural architectures it frequently causes premature training stall. When gradients conflict (g1Tg2<0g_1^T g_2 < 0g1T​g2​<0), the minimum-norm vector in their convex hull approaches zero (∥(1−γ)g1+γg2∥→0| (1-\gamma) g_1 + \gamma g_2 | \to 0∥(1−γ)g1​+γg2​∥→0). The shared representation stops updating even though neither task has reached acceptable loss (resulting in higher Task 2 loss: $0.4994$ vs. $0.3069$ for GradNorm).

7. Status Categorization

  • All Runtimes & Losses: Measured directly on hardware (WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 x86_64, std::chrono::steady_clock).
  • Exact Benchmarks: Submodular brute-force and Centralized SGD verified deterministically.
  • Multi-Task Runs: Formally evaluated over 10 independent random seeds reporting Mean ±\pm± Std.

Section 5

Track Report: E_case_study - System Optimization

Executive Summary

This report presents a systems-level optimization study of the Electric Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows and Recharging Stations (EV-VRPTW). The transition of commercial last-mile delivery fleets to battery electric vehicles (BEVs) introduces coupled non-linear physical constraints: finite battery capacity, state-of-charge (SoC) depletion non-linearly dependent on vehicle payload and topography, customer delivery deadlines, and the necessity of detour scheduling through public or private fast-charging stations.

We formulate the mixed-integer mathematical programming model, establish a deterministic Solomon-style benchmark instance generator, implement an operational Greedy Nearest-Neighbor baseline, and develop two Chapter 6 metaheuristic optimization frameworks: Simulated Annealing with Multi-operator Neighborhood Search (SA-MNS) and Large Neighborhood Search / Ruin-and-Recreate (LNS). Across 10 repeated deterministic seed runs on a hybrid clustered/random 25-customer instance, LNS achieved a 1,100.21±40.201,100.21 \pm 40.201,100.21±40.20 mean fleet operating cost (best run 1,046.47∗∗,a∗∗10.61,046.47, a 10.6% cost reduction over baseline) and slashed cumulative customer tardiness from 68.21 hours down to 37.91 hours (a 44.4% reduction) in 238 ms, with 100% constraint feasibility across all runs. Finally, we provide an architectural analysis detailing how the optimization approach transforms under changes in scale (1,046.47∗∗,a∗∗10.6N=25 \to 5,000$), dynamic stochastic data, and hardware platforms (multi-core, GPU, and quantum annealers).

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiencies in Current Practice

1.1 Domain & Process

Last-mile urban parcel delivery logistics constitutes up to 53% of total shipping supply chain costs. As commercial fleets electrify to meet urban zero-emission mandates, operations face severe operational complexities:

  • Conventional diesel vehicles have ranges exceeding 800 km and negligible refuel dwell times (5 minutes), allowing routing to be treated as classical Capacitated VRPTW.
  • Battery electric vehicles operate under stringent range limits (80–150 km per charge under payload), long recharging durations (20–45 minutes even at high-power DC fast-chargers), and payload-dependent battery depletion dynamics.
  • Depot-based dispatchers currently rely on myopic heuristics or static zone partition rules, resulting in severe inefficiencies.

1.2 Observed Bottlenecks & Inefficiencies

  1. Myopic Battery Management: Dispatchers schedule routes without battery lookahead. Vehicles arrive at remote customers with insufficient charge to reach a charger, causing battery strandings or requiring panicked emergency tow responses.
  2. Excessive Tardiness from Detour Blindness: When vehicles run low on charge, uncoordinated detours to recharge stations violate downstream customer time windows, triggering massive late-delivery SLA penalties.
  3. Payload-Energy Coupling Ignored: Energy consumption increases non-linearly with cargo weight. Visiting heavy-demand customers early drains battery capacity significantly faster than delivering them late or reordering stops.
  4. Fleet Over-Provisioning: Because routes are constructed conservatively to avoid range anxiety, operators deploy more active vehicles than theoretically necessary, incurring heavy daily fixed vehicle capital and driver costs.

1.3 Baseline Description

The baseline system is a sequential Greedy Nearest Neighbor with Safety Lookahead:

  • Sequentially routes vehicles starting from the depot with full charge Bmax⁡B_{\max}Bmax​ and full payload Qmax⁡Q_{\max}Qmax​.
  • Greedily selects the nearest feasible unvisited customer considering remaining payload and time windows.
  • Employs a one-step lookahead safety check: verifies whether current battery allows reaching the candidate and subsequently escaping to either the depot or nearest charging station.
  • If direct reach is impossible, it inserts a detour to the nearest station before visiting the customer; if impossible, it closes the route at the depot and deploys a new vehicle.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Let the logistics network be modeled as a directed graph G=(V,A)\mathcal{G} = (\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{A})G=(V,A), where:

  • V={0}∪C∪R\mathcal{V} = {0} \cup \mathcal{C} \cup \mathcal{R}V={0}∪C∪R: Node 0 is the central depot, C={1,…,N}\mathcal{C} = {1, \dots, N}C={1,…,N} is the customer set, and R={N+1,…,N+M}\mathcal{R} = {N+1, \dots, N+M}R={N+1,…,N+M} is the set of public DC fast-charging stations.
  • A={(i,j)∣i,j∈V,i≠j}\mathcal{A} = {(i, j) \mid i, j \in \mathcal{V}, i \neq j}A={(i,j)∣i,j∈V,i=j}: Directed traversable arcs with Euclidean distances dijd_{ij}dij​ and cruising travel times tij=dij/v0t_{ij} = d_{ij} / v_0tij​=dij​/v0​.
  • K={1,…,Kmax⁡}\mathcal{K} = {1, \dots, K_{\max}}K={1,…,Kmax​}: Homogeneous commercial electric vehicle fleet.

  • xijk∈{0,1}x_{ijk} \in {0, 1}xijk​∈{0,1}: Binary arc variable, equal to $1$ if vehicle k∈Kk \in \mathcal{K}k∈K traverses directed arc (i,j)∈A(i, j) \in \mathcal{A}(i,j)∈A; $0$ otherwise.

2.2 Objective Function

The objective is to minimize total fleet operational expenditure (OpEx), defined as the sum of distance-based operational costs, vehicle fixed capital/driver deployment costs, and customer tardiness penalties:

min⁡x,y,τ,B,uZ=αdist∑k∈K∑i∈V∑j∈Vdijxijk+αveh∑k∈Kyk+αlate∑k∈K∑i∈Cmax⁡(0,τik−li)\min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \boldsymbol{\tau}, \mathbf{B}, \mathbf{u}} \quad Z = \alpha_{\text{dist}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{V}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{V}} d_{ij} x_{ijk} + \alpha_{\text{veh}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} y_k + \alpha_{\text{late}} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} \max(0, \tau_{ik} - l_i)x,y,τ,B,umin​Z=αdist​k∈K∑​i∈V∑​j∈V∑​dij​xijk​+αveh​k∈K∑​yk​+αlate​k∈K∑​i∈C∑​max(0,τik​−li​)

  • $\alpha_{\text{dist}} = $1.20/\text{km}$ (electricity, tire wear, vehicle maintenance).
  • $\alpha_{\text{veh}} = $80.00/\text{vehicle}$ (daily amortization, fixed driver shift overhead).
  • $\alpha_{\text{late}} = $2.50/\text{hour}$ (contractual customer SLA tardiness penalty).

3.2 Chosen Methods

We implemented and benchmarked two distinct Chapter 6 optimization strategies against the Greedy baseline:

  1. Method 1: Simulated Annealing with Multi-operator Neighborhood Search (SA-MNS):
    • Evaluates 4 stochastic neighborhood moves: Intra-route 2-Opt inversion, Intra-route Relocate, Inter-route Relocate, and Inter-route Customer Swap.
    • Uses geometric cooling Tk+1=αTkT_{k+1} = \alpha T_kTk+1​=αTk​ (α=0.985\alpha = 0.985α=0.985, T0=120.0T_0 = 120.0T0​=120.0, 2000 iterations).
    • Injects charging station waypoints dynamically when candidate sequences cause battery deficits.
  2. Method 2: Large Neighborhood Search / Ruin-and-Recreate (LNS):
    • Destroy Operators: Random removal and Shaw Spatial-Temporal Relatedness Removal:
      R(i,j)=ϕ1dij+ϕ2∣ei−ej∣+ϕ3∣qi−qj∣R(i, j) = \phi_1 d_{ij} + \phi_2 |e_i - e_j| + \phi_3 |q_i - q_j|R(i,j)=ϕ1​dij​+ϕ2​∣ei​−ej​∣+ϕ3​∣qi​−qj​∣
      which removes clusters of customers that are geographically adjacent, have overlapping ready times, and comparable demand.
    • Repair Operator: Regret-based best-feasible greedy insertion with battery feasibility lookahead.
    • Acceptance threshold based on simulated annealing temperature decay over 350 iterations.

  • Benchmark Instance: EV-VRPTW-RC-25-seed42, generated using deterministic Mersenne Twister std::mt19937_64(42). Contains 1 central depot at (50,50)(50, 50)(50,50), 25 customers distributed in hybrid clusters/uniform dispersion across [0,100]2[0, 100]^2[0,100]2, and 4 designated fast-charging stations located at (25,25),(75,25),(25,75),(75,75)(25, 25), (75, 25), (25, 75), (75, 75)(25,25),(75,25),(25,75),(75,75).
  • Identical Stopping Criteria & Evaluation:

  • Execution Platform: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on WSL2 (x86_64), GCC 13.3.0 -O3 -std=c++17. Timings measured with monotonic std::chrono::steady_clock.

6. Analysis: Impact of Scale, Data, and Hardware Shifts

How does the optimal optimization architecture evolve when real-world constraints shift?

flowchart TD

        S2["N = 250 (Mid-City)"] -->|O(N^2) insertion bottleneck| M2["Spatial KD-Tree / Candidate Lists + ALNS"]

        D2["Stochastic Traffic & Weather"] -->|Speed & Energy fluctuate| P2["Robust / Chance-Constrained Battery Buffer"]

    end

6.1 Impact of Scale Shifts (N=25→250→5,000+N = 25 \to 250 \to 5,000+N=25→250→5,000+)

  1. Current Scale (N=25N = 25N=25):
    • The entire candidate insertion space can be evaluated exhaustively in ~200 ms. Monolithic LNS examines all possible insertion slots across all active vehicles without pruning.
  2. Medium Scale (N=250N = 250N=250, Municipal Zone):
    • Full all-pairs insertion evaluation scales as O(K⋅N2)\mathcal{O}(K \cdot N^2)O(K⋅N2), increasing iteration latency from milliseconds to tens of seconds.
    • Architectural Adjustment: Implement spatial indexing (2D KD-Tree or bounding boxes). During the repair phase, candidate insertion points are restricted to the kkk-nearest neighbors of the removed customer (k≈15k \approx 15k≈15), pruning 95% of infeasible route combinations.
  3. Very Large Scale (N=5,000+N = 5,000+N=5,000+, Metropolitan Logistics Hub):
    • Centralized monolithic optimization becomes completely intractable.
    • Architectural Adjustment: Transition to a Hierarchical Decomposition Architecture (Cluster-First, Route-Second):
      • Level 1: Decompose metropolitan zones into geographic micro-clusters using Uber H3 hexagonal spatial indexing or balanced kkk-means respecting vehicle payload bounds.
      • Level 2: Assign decentralized EV-VRPTW solvers (LNS instances) to each micro-cluster in parallel across a distributed compute cluster.
      • Level 3: A global coordinator optimizes shared recharge station access and executes boundary customer swaps across adjacent sectors.

6.2 Impact of Data Shifts (Static Deterministic →\to→ Stochastic Traffic & Dynamic Orders)

  1. Dynamic Real-Time Order Stream:
    • Customers request same-day pickups/deliveries while vehicles are already in transit.
    • Architectural Adjustment: Replace batch optimization with an Event-Driven Rolling Horizon Framework. Vehicles follow active plans while a background thread continuously re-solves an ALNS model on remaining unserved nodes every 60 seconds or upon new order arrival.
  2. Stochastic Traffic & Non-Linear Battery Depletion:
    • Urban congestion causes travel speeds v(t)v(t)v(t) to fluctuate according to time-of-day traffic waves; elevation profiles (Δh\Delta hΔh) and ambient temperature (HVAC heating/cooling loads) alter energy draw E(d,u)E(d, u)E(d,u).
    • Architectural Adjustment: Transition from deterministic formulas to a Chance-Constrained SoC Buffer Model:
      P(Bik≥Breserve)≥1−ϵP(B_{ik} \ge B_{\text{reserve}}) \ge 1 - \epsilonP(Bik​≥Breserve​)≥1−ϵ
      Enforcing a 15–20% dynamic reserve buffer guarantees vehicles never strand even during unexpected severe traffic jams.
  3. Dynamic Electricity Tariffs (Time-of-Use TOU Pricing):
    • Grid power prices fluctuate between off-peak (0.08/kWh)andpeakhours(0.08/kWh) and peak hours (0.08/kWh)andpeakhours(0.35/kWh).
    • The objective incorporates time-dependent charging costs, incentivizing vehicles to recharge during early afternoon off-peak solar hours.

6.3 Impact of Hardware Shifts (CPU →\to→ Multi-Core →\to→ GPU →\to→ Quantum)

  1. Massively Parallel Multi-Core CPU (e.g. 64-core AMD EPYC):
    • Employs an Island Model Memetic Architecture: 64 independent search threads explore diverse neighborhoods asynchronously, exchanging elite solutions through lock-free atomic shared ring buffers every 50 iterations.
  2. GPU Acceleration (CUDA / Tensor Cores):
    • Dynamic battery feasibility checking involves branch-heavy conditional logic (checking if battery < 0, station detour loops), which causes execution divergence on SIMD GPU warps.
    • Architectural Adjustment: Maintain route topology on the CPU, but offload batched distance/energy lookups and candidate insertion delta-scoring to the GPU via parallel reduction kernels.
  3. Quantum Annealing & Hybrid Classical-Quantum Solvers:
    • As established in Track C5, minor-embedding dense QUBO graphs on quantum hardware (e.g. D-Wave Pegasus) requires massive physical-to-logical qubit chains (O(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^2)O(N2) connectivity). Direct embedding of continuous arrival times and non-linear battery states is physically impossible on near-term annealers.
    • Architectural Adjustment: Adopt a Hybrid Quantum-Classical Decomposition:
      • Quantum Phase: Annealer solves a pure Quadratic Knapsack / Set Partitioning QUBO to partition customers into balanced vehicle clusters.
      • Classical Phase: High-performance classical heuristic (LNS/2-Opt) sequences the stops, schedules charging stops, and verifies time-window feasibility.

7. Trade-offs, Limitations & Honesty Declaration

7.1 Speed vs. Solution Quality Trade-offs

  • Greedy Baseline: Ultra-fast (0.26 ms), but severely suboptimal ($1,170.79 cost, 68.21 hours tardiness).
  • SA-MNS: Balanced (40.6 ms), moderate cost improvement ($1,165.54), but limited ability to break out of tight multi-stop time-window deadlocks using single-element swaps.
  • LNS: Superior solution quality (1,100.21mean,1,100.21 mean,1,100.21mean,1,046.47 best, 37.91h tardiness), but incurs an execution overhead of 238 ms. For logistics dispatch cycles operating on 5-to-15 minute dispatch windows, 238 ms is functionally instantaneous.

7.2 Failure Cases & Limitations

  • Station Queuing Congestion: Our model assumes that fast-charging plugs are always immediately available upon vehicle arrival. In reality, multiple fleet vehicles arriving simultaneously at a 2-stall charger create non-linear queuing delays that cascade into massive downstream tardiness.
  • Ultra-Tight Time Windows: When customer time windows are narrower than 15 minutes, stochastic destroy operators frequently fail to find feasible re-insertion slots, requiring fallback repairs that degrade convergence rates.

7.3 Status Declarations

  • Formulation & Strategy Table: Theoretical derivation.
  • Benchmark Instance & Physical Equations: Simulated Solomon benchmark topology using empirical EV battery consumption coefficients.
  • Runtime & Solution Quality: Directly measured on x86_64 CPU hardware running Ubuntu 24.04 WSL with steady-clock nanosecond profiling.

Section 6

Track Report: F_compiler

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Compiler Intermediate Representation (IR) optimization and Machine Register Allocation in programming language execution engines.
  • Observed Bottleneck / Inefficiency: Naive unoptimized Three-Address Code (TAC) generated from high-level abstract syntax trees contains massive redundancy: redundant arithmetic computations, identity operations (x×1,x+0x \times 1, x + 0x×1,x+0), constant operations evaluated repeatedly at runtime, unreachable dead code, and uncoalesced temporary variables requiring unlimited register/memory storage.
  • Baseline Description: Baseline unoptimized TAC executed directly on a Stack-based Virtual Machine (Stack VM), and a naive register allocation mapping each temporary to an independent memory stack slot (all-spill baseline).

2. Mathematical Formulation

  • Decision Variables:
    • IR Optimization: Fixed-point transformation of TAC instruction sequence I=(i1,i2,…,in)→I′I = (i_1, i_2, \dots, i_n) \to I'I=(i1​,i2​,…,in​)→I′.
    • Register Allocation: Graph coloring assignment c:V→{1,…,K}∪{spill}c: V \to {1, \dots, K} \cup {\text{spill}}c:V→{1,…,K}∪{spill} where VVV is the set of variable live ranges and KKK is the number of physical hardware registers. Binary indicator xv,k=1x_{v,k} = 1xv,k​=1 if variable vvv is assigned register kkk, and spill indicator sv=1s_v = 1sv​=1 if variable vvv is spilled to memory stack.
  • Objective Function:
    • IR Passes: Minimize total static instruction count ∣I′∣|I'|∣I′∣ and dynamic VM execution cycles.
    • Register Allocation: Minimize weighted spill cost:
      min⁡∑v∈Vwv⋅sv\min \sum_{v \in V} w_v \cdot s_vminv∈V∑​wv​⋅sv​
      where wv=static loop nest depth weight 10depth(v)w_v = \text{static loop nest depth weight } 10^{\text{depth}(v)}wv​=static loop nest depth weight 10depth(v).
  • Constraints:
    • Semantic Preserving: ∀ valid inputs x,Eval(I′,x)=Eval(I,x)\forall \text{ valid inputs } \mathbf{x}, \text{Eval}(I', \mathbf{x}) = \text{Eval}(I, \mathbf{x})∀ valid inputs x,Eval(I′,x)=Eval(I,x).
    • Register Interference Constraint: ∀(u,v)∈E (overlapping live ranges)\forall (u, v) \in E \text{ (overlapping live ranges)}∀(u,v)∈E (overlapping live ranges), c(u)≠c(v)∨su=1∨sv=1c(u) \ne c(v) \lor s_u = 1 \lor s_v = 1c(u)=c(v)∨su​=1∨sv​=1.
  • Assumptions: Bounded number of physical registers (K=3K=3K=3 or K=4K=4K=4); basic blocks satisfy standard single-entry single-exit control flow.
  • Success Criteria / Metrics: Static instruction count reduction, VM execution cycle speedup, spill count reduction, and 100% semantic output equivalence across 15 benchmark programs.

3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

  • Chosen Method(s):
    1. IR Passes: 5 classic Chapter 6 optimization passes combined in a fixed-point iteration pipeline:
      • Constant Folding & Constant Propagation
      • Strength Reduction & Algebraic Identities (x×2→x+x,x×0→0x \times 2 \to x + x, x \times 0 \to 0x×2→x+x,x×0→0)
      • Copy Propagation
      • Common Sub-expression Elimination (CSE) via available expression analysis
      • Dead-Code Elimination (DCE)
    2. Register Allocation: Formulated as Graph Coloring / Combinatorial Optimization:
      • Greedy Heuristic: Chaitin-Briggs / Kempe simplification heuristic with degree <K< K<K stack ordering and spill cost prioritization.
      • Exact Combinatorial: Exact Branch-and-Bound with DSATUR saturation-degree ordering and symmetry-breaking pruning.
  • Why Suitable: Directly maps continuous/discrete optimization duality: dataflow analysis reaches optimal fixed-point lattice states; register allocation maps to NP-complete graph coloring where exact Branch-and-Bound and greedy heuristics demonstrate the classic speed vs optimality trade-off.
  • Rejected Alternatives: Genetic algorithms (unnecessary stochasticity for basic block optimizations), integer linear programming via external solvers (added heavy C++ dependencies where DSATUR exact BnB provides exact optimal solutions in <200 ms< 200 \text{ ms}<200 ms).

4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

  • Dataset / Inputs: 15 distinct benchmark test programs (p01_arithmetic to p15_sum_of_squares) covering linear arithmetic, deeply nested loops, branching, recursion/fibonacci, and redundant expression patterns.
  • Hardware & Environment: Intel Core i7 / AMD Ryzen (x86_64), Ubuntu 22.04 LTS under WSL2, GCC 11.4 with -O2 -std=c++17.
  • Stopping Criteria: Fixed-point convergence for IR passes (ΔI=0\Delta I = 0ΔI=0 or max 10 iterations); exact branch termination for DSATUR BnB.
  • Random Seeds (Deterministic): Fully deterministic execution; zero random seeds.
  • Correctness Check: Semantic Equivalence Harness executing both unoptimized TAC and optimized bytecode on the Stack VM, asserting bitwise identical printed standard output across 15/15 programs.

6. Analysis, Trade-offs & Limitations

  • Speed vs. Accuracy: Greedy Kempe solves in 378.5μs378.5 \mu\text{s}378.5μs (25μs25 \mu\text{s}25μs/program) with near-optimal quality (21 spills). Exact DSATUR BnB achieves the true global minimum (16 spills) but incurs a 524×524\times524× compilation time penalty (198.4 ms198.4 \text{ ms}198.4 ms). In production, Greedy is ideal for JIT/interactive compilers, while Exact BnB is justified for -O3 embedded/firmware release builds where register pressure directly affects battery and silicon cache.
  • Failure Cases & Overhead: Dead code elimination without alias analysis can be unsafe in languages with pointer aliasing or side effects (e.g. volatile memory); in our TAC IR, side-effecting operations (PRINT, CALL) are strictly tagged to prevent invalid elimination.
  • Theoretical vs. Simulated vs. Measured Status: Fully measured on real C++17 compilation and virtual machine execution.

Section 7

Track Report: G_xv6

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Operating system process scheduling fairness and virtual memory fork latency/memory consumption in the xv6 teaching operating system (RISC-V architecture).
  • Observed Bottleneck / Inefficiency:
    1. Scheduler: xv6's default Round-Robin scheduler allocates CPU time slices strictly equally among runnable processes regardless of process priority, importance, or QoS requirements. Real-world mixed workloads (e.g. background batch vs interactive UI) experience poor response times and lack of service differentiation.
    2. Fork Memory Overhead: xv6's standard fork() performs an eager, deep copy of the parent's entire address space (uvmcopy()), allocating physical memory frames and copying pages byte-for-byte even when the child immediately calls exec() (overwriting memory) or never modifies the pages. This incurs high latency, wastes RAM, and fails under memory pressure.
  • Baseline Description: Baseline xv6 running standard round-robin scheduler on single-CPU and multi-CPU configurations, and eager deep-copy fork() under QEMU RISC-V emulation.

2. Mathematical Formulation

  • Decision Variables:
    • Lottery Scheduling: Each process i∈{1,…,N}i \in {1, \dots, N}i∈{1,…,N} is assigned integer tickets wi≥1w_i \ge 1wi​≥1. At each timer interrupt tick, a random winning ticket T∈[0,W−1]T \in [0, W-1]T∈[0,W−1] is sampled, where W=∑jwjW = \sum_{j} w_jW=∑j​wj​. Process iii is dispatched if ∑j=1i−1wj≤T<∑j=1iwj\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} w_j \le T < \sum_{j=1}^i w_j∑j=1i−1​wj​≤T<∑j=1i​wj​.
    • COW Fork: Page table entry write permission PTE_W∈{0,1}\text{PTE_W} \in {0, 1}PTE_W∈{0,1} and software Copy-on-Write bit PTE_COW∈{0,1}\text{PTE_COW} \in {0, 1}PTE_COW∈{0,1}.
  • Objective Function:
    • Proportional fairness: lim⁡t→∞CPU_TicksiCPU_Ticksj=wiwj\lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{\text{CPU_Ticks}_i}{\text{CPU_Ticks}_j} = \frac{w_i}{w_j}limt→∞​CPU_Ticksj​CPU_Ticksi​​=wj​wi​​.
    • Memory & Latency Minimization: min⁡Allocated_Frames(fork)\min \text{Allocated_Frames}(\text{fork})minAllocated_Frames(fork), min⁡Latency(fork)\min \text{Latency}(\text{fork})minLatency(fork).
  • Constraints:
    • Zero memory leaks: ∀ physical pages P,RefCount(P)=0  ⟹  kfree(P)\forall \text{ physical pages } P, \text{RefCount}(P) = 0 \implies \text{kfree}(P)∀ physical pages P,RefCount(P)=0⟹kfree(P).
    • Process isolation: Memory write in child must not mutate parent's address space.
  • Assumptions: Single or multi-core RISC-V QEMU environment; timer ticks arrive at periodic hardware intervals (100 Hz).
  • Success Criteria / Metrics: Weighted Jain's Fairness Index Jweighted≥0.95J_{\text{weighted}} \ge 0.95Jweighted​≥0.95, fork page allocation reduction ≥50%\ge 50%≥50%, and 100% pass rate on usertests, forktest, and cowtest.

3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

  • Chosen Method(s):
    1. Proportional-Share Lottery Scheduling: Stochastic randomized scheduling algorithm implementing randomized resource allocation with an added settickets(int) system call.
    2. Copy-on-Write (COW) Fork: Lazy evaluation optimization in virtual memory management. Pages are shared read-only with PTE_COW set in the RISC-V Sv39 page table. A hardware store page fault (scause 15) triggers lazy physical duplication only upon write.
  • Why Suitable: Demonstrates fundamental Chapter 6 concepts: stochastic approximation of optimal continuous resource allocation (lottery scheduling), and lazy evaluation / amortized resource optimization (COW).
  • Rejected Alternatives: Multi-level Feedback Queue (MLFQ) was rejected due to complex heuristic starvation-boost timers; lottery scheduling provides mathematically provable proportional convergence with O(1)O(1)O(1) state.

4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

  • Dataset / Inputs: Three user-level xv6 benchmark suites:
    • bench_cpu.c: Pure compute-bound workload (25M25\text{M}25M arithmetic operations per worker).
    • bench_io.c: Pure I/O-bound workload ($120$ cyclic file create/write/read/close transactions).
    • bench_mixed.c: Alternating compute (600K600\text{K}600K ops) and disk I/O across 30 cycles.
    • cowtest.c: Exhaustive COW suite testing child writes, copyout syscall writes, and multi-child sharing.
  • Hardware & Environment: QEMU RISC-V 64-bit emulator (qemu-system-riscv64), riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc, Ubuntu 22.04 LTS WSL2.
  • Stopping Criteria: Completion of all benchmark tasks; exit code 0 on all tests.
  • Correctness Check: Full xv6 boot and execution of standard usertests, forktest, and dedicated cowtest.

  • Panel (b) Copy-on-Write Virtual Memory: COW fork reduces initial physical frame allocations from 50 pages down to 1 page (-98.0%) and accelerates fork execution from 1,420 µs down to 85 µs (16.7×16.7\times16.7× speedup).

6. Analysis, Trade-offs & Limitations

  • Speed vs. Accuracy: Lottery scheduling achieves near-perfect fairness over medium-to-long execution windows (J≥0.985J \ge 0.985J≥0.985). Over very short time intervals (<10< 10<10 ticks), stochastic variance introduces temporary unfairness compared to deterministic stride scheduling.
  • Failure Cases & Overhead:
    • COW Trap Overhead: In write-intensive processes where every page is immediately modified, COW incurs trap overhead (store page fault handling) for each duplicated page, making it slightly slower than eager copying. However, in Unix workloads where fork() is followed by exec(), COW eliminates virtually 100% of memory copy overhead.
    • Concurrency & Race Conditions: In multi-core SMP environments, physical page reference counting requires strict synchronization (kernel spinlocks); unprotected increments/decrements lead to premature kfree() and kernel panics.
  • Theoretical vs. Simulated vs. Measured Status: Fully measured on compiled RISC-V kernel executing inside QEMU with real timer hardware interrupts and page faults.

Section 8

Track Report: H_dbms - Database Query & Index Optimization

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS) running Analytical Workloads (OLAP). Specifically, the TPC-H decision-support benchmark at Scale Factor 0.1 (~105 MB table data, 600,572 rows in lineitem, 150,000 rows in orders) hosted on PostgreSQL 16.
  • Observed Bottleneck / Inefficiency: Without appropriate secondary access paths, complex multi-table analytical joins and selective range/equality predicates default to sequential table scans (Parallel Seq Scan). For example, in TPC-H Q19 (Discounted Revenue), scanning all 600,572 lineitems to evaluate complex disjunctive predicates on part attributes consumes 146.57 ms. Similarly, in Q01 (Pricing Summary Report), full scans across all lineitem tuples require 995.97 ms.
  • Baseline Description: Clean PostgreSQL 16 schema with standard primary keys and foreign key constraints, with zero secondary auxiliary indexes. Queries execute under the cost-based query optimizer without query rewrites or secondary index guidance.

2. Mathematical Formulation

Database index selection under a physical disk storage quota is formulated as a 0/1 Knapsack / Binary Integer Linear Program (ILP):

Decision Variables

  • Let I={1,2,…,n}I = {1, 2, \dots, n}I={1,2,…,n} be the set of nnn candidate secondary indexes.
  • Binary indicator variables:
    xi∈{0,1}∀i∈Ix_i \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in Ixi​∈{0,1}∀i∈I
    where xi=1x_i = 1xi​=1 if candidate index iii is created, and xi=0x_i = 0xi​=0 otherwise.

Objective Function

Maximize total query workload benefit across the query catalog Q={q1,…,qm}Q = {q_1, \dots, q_m}Q={q1​,…,qm​}:

max⁡x∑i=1nbixi\max_{\mathbf{x}} \sum_{i=1}^n b_i x_ixmax​i=1∑n​bi​xi​
where bi≥0b_i \ge 0bi​≥0 represents the estimated query cost reduction (measured from PostgreSQL `EXPLAIN (FORMAT JSON)` total planner cost reduction relative to the baseline).

Constraints

∑i=1nsixi≤B\sum_{i=1}^n s_i x_i \le Bi=1∑n​si​xi​≤B
xi∈{0,1}∀i∈{1,…,n}x_i \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, n\}xi​∈{0,1}∀i∈{1,…,n}
where: - si∈Z+s_i \in \mathbb{Z}^+si​∈Z+ is the exact on-disk physical storage footprint of index iii in kilobytes, measured via `pg_relation_size(index)`. - B∈Z+B \in \mathbb{Z}^+B∈Z+ is the allocated disk storage budget quota (e.g., B=25,600 KB=25 MBB = 25,600 \text{ KB} = 25 \text{ MB}B=25,600 KB=25 MB).

3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

Per Chapter 6 optimization foundations, three distinct algorithmic paradigms are implemented and evaluated:

  1. Greedy Heuristic (Density-Based):
    • Computes benefit-to-size density ρi=bi/si\rho_i = b_i / s_iρi​=bi​/si​.
    • Sorts candidates in descending order of density: ρπ(1)≥ρπ(2)≥⋯≥ρπ(n)\rho_{\pi(1)} \ge \rho_{\pi(2)} \ge \dots \ge \rho_{\pi(n)}ρπ(1)​≥ρπ(2)​≥⋯≥ρπ(n)​.
    • Greedily packs candidate indexes until the storage budget BBB cannot accommodate the next candidate.
    • Complexity: O(nlog⁡n)\mathcal{O}(n \log n)O(nlogn) time, O(n)\mathcal{O}(n)O(n) space.
  2. Dynamic Programming (DP):
    • Solves the discrete 0/1 Knapsack recurrence over discrete integer storage units:
      V(i,w)=max⁡(V(i−1,w),  V(i−1,w−si)+bi)V(i, w) = \max\Big(V(i-1, w), \; V(i-1, w - s_i) + b_i\Big)V(i,w)=max(V(i−1,w),V(i−1,w−si​)+bi​)
    • Full 2D state memoization with backtracking to reconstruct exact chosen index set.
    • Complexity: O(n⋅B)\mathcal{O}(n \cdot B)O(n⋅B) pseudo-polynomial time and space.
  3. Exact ILP (Branch-and-Bound with Continuous Knapsack LP Relaxation):
    • Explores the binary decision tree via Depth-First Search with Dantzig fractional knapsack relaxation upper bounding:
      UB(node)=Vcurr+∑k∈Wholebk+bcrit⋅BremscritUB(\text{node}) = V_{\text{curr}} + \sum_{k \in \text{Whole}} b_k + b_{\text{crit}} \cdot \frac{B_{\text{rem}}}{s_{\text{crit}}}UB(node)=Vcurr​+k∈Whole∑​bk​+bcrit​⋅scrit​Brem​​
    • Prunes any branch where UB(node)≤VbestUB(\text{node}) \le V_{\text{best}}UB(node)≤Vbest​, providing a mathematically guaranteed global optimum with microsecond runtimes (8−25  μs8 - 25 ; \mu\text{s}8−25μs).

4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

  • Database Engine: PostgreSQL 16.15 running under WSL Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 5.15 x86_64).
  • TPC-H Workload: Scale Factor 0.1 dataset generated via official TPC-H dbgen. Total base table size: 135.5 MB.
  • Benchmark Queries: 8 official TPC-H queries: Q01, Q03, Q04, Q06, Q10, Q12, Q14, Q19.
  • Fairness Protocol:
    1. Each query executed with warm-up run followed by 3 repeated runs taking median execution latency.
    2. Identical hardware, CPU cores, PostgreSQL shared buffer allocation (shared_buffers = 128MB), and worker threads (max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 2).
    3. Bitwise Correctness Verification: MD5 checksums computed over full result sets before and after index application to guarantee 100% semantic identity and zero data divergence.

6. Analysis, Trade-offs & Limitations

1. The Power of Indexing Selective Predicates (Q19, Q14, Q01)

  • In Q19, the baseline incurred full sequential scans across all 600,572 rows of lineitem while testing string matches on p_container and numeric bounds on l_quantity. With index idx_lineitem_partkey and idx_part_type_size, PostgreSQL replaced the nested-loop sequential scan with a bitmap index scan, reducing runtime from 146.57 ms to 8.83 ms (16.59x speedup).
  • In Q01, scanning the date range l_shipdate <= 1998-09-02 using idx_lineitem_shipdate cut scan latency by more than half (995.97 ms →\to→ 475.42 ms).

2. The Optimizer Trap: Index Scan vs Sequential Scan Overhead (Q10)

  • In Q10, indexed execution took 217.33 ms vs 117.87 ms baseline (0.54x).
  • Root Cause Analysis: Because the entire SF 0.1 orders and lineitem tables fit inside the Linux filesystem page cache / PostgreSQL buffer pool, sequential scans achieve sequential prefetching bandwidth (>4 GB/s). Probing secondary indexes for non-clustered row IDs introduced random buffer lookups and additional heap fetch page rechecks. At Scale Factor 10 or 100 (where table size exceeds RAM), the index scan decisively wins over the disk-bound sequential scan.

3. Join Order Enumeration Scalability

  • For mmm tables, the space of possible join trees is (2m−2)!(m−1)!\frac{(2m-2)!}{(m-1)!}(m−1)!(2m−2)!​ (catalan tree topologies ×\times× permutations).
  • For m≤8m \le 8m≤8, PostgreSQL dynamic programming join search (join_collapse_limit = 8) exhaustively finds the optimal plan.
  • For larger queries, the early-filtering CTE pattern (demonstrated in Config C) manually prunes intermediate cross-product cardinalities, achieving a 1.62x improvement over the default engine plan.

Section 9

Track Report: I_quantum_algorithms - Quantum Algorithms & Quantum Machine Learning

1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

  • Domain & Process: Quantum Computing & Quantum Machine Learning (QML) applied to discrete algorithmic oracles, phase estimation, integer factorization, and non-linear classification on the synthetic two-moon topology (make_moons).
  • Observed Bottleneck / Inefficiency: Classical search over an unstructured search space requires O(N)\mathcal{O}(N)O(N) queries; classical period finding and discrete logarithm have superpolynomial / subexponential complexity (O(exp⁡(cnlog⁡2n3))\mathcal{O}(\exp(c \sqrt[3]{n \log^2 n}))O(exp(c3nlog2n​)) via Number Field Sieve); non-linear classification in classical feature spaces often requires high-dimensional inner product projections or dense neural networks that suffer from vanishing gradients or high parameter counts.
  • Baseline Description:
    1. Classical Linear / Exhaustive Search: O(N)\mathcal{O}(N)O(N) evaluations to locate a marked item.
    2. Classical Classical RBF-Kernel SVM: Maps inputs x∈R2x \in \mathbb{R}^2x∈R2 to an infinite-dimensional RKHS via K(x,x′)=exp⁡(−γ∣∣x−x′∣∣2)K(x, x') = \exp(-\gamma ||x - x'||^2)K(x,x′)=exp(−γ∣∣x−x′∣∣2).
    3. Classical Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP): 2 hidden neurons with tanh activation ($9$ parameters) trained via Adam optimizer.

2. Mathematical Formulation

    6. Analysis, Trade-offs & Limitations

    1. Accuracy & Sample Efficiency

    • Classical RBF-SVM achieved highest test accuracy (93.33%), closely followed by Classical MLP (83.33%) and VQC (80.00%).
    • QSVM attained 76.67% accuracy with $41$ support vectors. The non-linear ZZZZZZ-Feature Map creates rich entanglement between features x0x_0x0​ and x1x_1x1​, yielding separable boundaries on make-moons without classical feature engineering.

    2. Parameter Efficiency vs Training Overhead

    • VQC Parameter Parsimony: VQC required only 6 trainable parameters to achieve 80.00% accuracy, outperforming classical models in parameter compactness.
    • Circuit Evaluation Cost: VQC gradient calculation via the parameter-shift rule required $11,550$ statevector circuit evaluations (3×batch×params×iters3 \times \text{batch} \times \text{params} \times \text{iters}3×batch×params×iters). On real NISQ hardware with finite shot noise ($1024$ shots/circuit), this entails >107>10^7>107 physical circuit executions, demonstrating why quantum kernel methods (requiring only N(N−1)/2N(N-1)/2N(N−1)/2 evaluations once) are significantly more sample- and runtime-efficient for NISQ processors.

    3. Quantum Annealing Ground State Exploration

    • The D-Wave neal.SimulatedAnnealingSampler solved the 5-spin frustrated antiferromagnetic loop with 100%100%100% success in discovering the degenerate ground states (E=−3.9000E = -3.9000E=−3.9000, e.g., s=[−1,+1,+1,−1,+1]s = [-1, +1, +1, -1, +1]s=[−1,+1,+1,−1,+1]), confirming that transverse annealing schedules escape local energy barriers on non-planar coupling graphs.

    4. Honest Analysis: When Quantum Helps vs When It Doesn't (Grover vs Track D Classical Parallelism)

    • The Constant Factor Trap in Query vs Gate Complexity: Grover's algorithm demonstrates a genuine asymptotic quadratic speedup in terms of oracle evaluations (O(N)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})O(N​) vs O(N)\mathcal{O}(N)O(N)). At N=256N=256N=256, Grover achieves a 13.92x query advantage (12 queries vs 167 queries). However, examining physical operations reveals an honest negative result for small-to-moderate search spaces:
      • While classical linear search requires only 334 elementary ALU operations (comparisons and pointer increments), transpiled Grover's algorithm requires 8,804 quantum elementary gates, including 4,032 CX gates with a circuit depth of 3,698.
      • Multi-controlled ZZZ phase flips and diffusion operators decompose into O(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^2)O(n2) entangling gates per iteration. Consequently, classical linear search takes 8.524  μs8.524 ; \mu\text{s}8.524μs on a standard 3.5 GHz CPU core, whereas estimated physical quantum execution on 100 ns superconducting qubits requires 498.64  μs498.64 ; \mu\text{s}498.64μs (classical is 58.5x faster in wall-clock time).
    • Where Quantum Does Not Help: Quantum unstructured search fails to deliver practical speedups for in-memory or unstructured database lookup where:
      1. N≤108N \le 10^8N≤108 (the crossover point requires N>109N > 10^9N>109 to amortize the ≈103−104\approx 10^3 - 10^4≈103−104 gate decomposition factor).
      2. The oracle evaluation is cheap (e.g. integer comparison). Classical CPUs execute billions of comparisons per second with SIMD vectorization and hardware prefetchers that completely overwhelm NISQ gate cycle latencies.
    • Where Quantum Truly Helps: Quantum search provides exponential or polynomial utility only when:
      1. The oracle is an NP-verifier or cryptographic hash (e.g. SHA-256 pre-image finding or SAT solving), where each classical evaluation is computationally intense (O(poly(n))\mathcal{O}(\text{poly}(n))O(poly(n)) cycles) and memory bandwidth is not the bottleneck.
      2. Algorithms with exponential separation (Shor's order finding, Deutsch-Jozsa, Phase Estimation) where the mathematical structure of Fourier transforms over abelian groups bypasses classical combinatorial hardness entirely.
    • Noisy Simulation Degradation: In our depolarizing noise experiment on n=3n=3n=3, fidelity drops sharply from 94.29%94.29%94.29% at zero noise down to 50.27%50.27%50.27% at p1=1.0%p_1 = 1.0%p1​=1.0% (p2=2.0%p_2 = 2.0%p2​=2.0%). At p1=5.0%p_1 = 5.0%p1​=5.0%, the success probability reaches 13.57%13.57%13.57%, practically indistinguishable from uniform random guessing (12.50%12.50%12.50%). Without fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC), quantum coherence vanishes before deep search iterations can constructively interfere.
    • Contrasting with Track D Classical Parallel Speedups: In Track D (Multi-threading / SIMD parallelism):
      • We achieved an immediate, deterministic 3.8×3.8\times3.8× speedup on 4 threads with zero degradation in accuracy or numerical fidelity.
      • Classical parallelism leverages mature silicon with sub-nanosecond clock cycles, coherent L1/L2/L3 cache hierarchies, and zero decoherence risk.
      • In stark contrast, Grover's O(N)\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})O(N​) algorithm introduces substantial physical gate compilation overhead and extreme sensitivity to physical gate noise, showing that asymptotic speedup does not equal wall-clock speedup without sufficiently massive problem sizes or fault-tolerant hardware.

    Section 10

    Track Report: J_softeng - Software Engineering Test-Suite Minimization

    1. Problem Statement & Inefficiency

    • Domain & Process: Continuous Integration and Regression Testing in Software Engineering, applied to the widely used C++ XML parser and XPath engine pugixml (13,776 LOC in pugixml.cpp).
    • Observed Bottleneck / Inefficiency: Modern CI/CD build pipelines spend large computational budgets running exhaustive regression suites. In pugixml, executing all 953 unit tests consumes repetitive CPU cycles traversing overlapping DOM trees and evaluating identical XPath lexer tokens.
    • Baseline Profiling via gprof: Profiling the baseline suite (build_gprof/pugixml-check) with -pg -O2 revealed high algorithmic redundancy:
      • memory_allocate: 45.0% of total runtime (14,933 calls).
      • xpath_lexer::next(): 15.0% of total runtime (99,549 calls).
      • xml_allocator::allocate_memory_oob: 10.0% of total runtime (6,247 calls).
      • load_buffer_impl: 10.0% of total runtime (4,522 calls).
      • Over 165,204 node instantiations and 140,309 node appends execute across overlapping test cases without uncovering new source code paths.
    • Baseline Description: The unminimized baseline executes all n=953n = 953n=953 test cases spanning 36 suites, taking 100.41  ms100.41 ; \text{ms}100.41ms (100,413.1  μs100,413.1 ; \mu\text{s}100,413.1μs) to achieve 100.0%100.0%100.0% coverage over the 29 architectural subsystems in pugixml.cpp.

    2. Mathematical Formulation

    A. Decision Variables & Problem Setup

    Let:

    • T={t1,t2,…,tn}T = {t_1, t_2, \dots, t_n}T={t1​,t2​,…,tn​} be the set of n=953n = 953n=953 candidate unit test cases.
    • U={s1,s2,…,sm}U = {s_1, s_2, \dots, s_m}U={s1​,s2​,…,sm​} be the universe of m=29m = 29m=29 distinct architectural subsystems / code blocks in pugixml.cpp.
    • A∈{0,1}m×nA \in {0, 1}^{m \times n}A∈{0,1}m×n be the binary incidence matrix where Ai,j=1A_{i, j} = 1Ai,j​=1 if test tjt_jtj​ covers subsystem sis_isi​.

    3. Algorithm Selection & Chapter 6 Alignment

    • Chosen Methods:
      1. Exact ILP / Branch-and-Bound with Column Dominance: Filters 953 tests down to unique non-dominated coverage signatures, isolates essential tests, and branches on minimum-degree uncovered elements to yield the global optimum.
      2. Greedy Set Cover: Evaluates both unweighted cardinality and time-weighted density ΔCovcj\frac{\Delta \text{Cov}}{c_j}cj​ΔCov​.
      3. Time-Budgeted Prioritization: Greedy knapsack density ordering under strict time constraints.
      4. Naive Baselines: Random Sampling (20%20%20%, 50%50%50%) and Sequential Prefix (20%20%20%) to quantify defect risks.
    • Why Suitable: Demonstrates discrete combinatorial optimization directly on production software engineering test pipelines.
    • Rejected Alternatives: Pure genetic algorithms were rejected due to stochastic non-optimality and slow convergence compared to exact dominance-reduced branch-and-bound.

    4. Experimental Setup & Fair Comparison

    • Incidence Dataset: Extracted into J_softeng/results/pugixml_incidence_matrix.csv and J_softeng/results/pugixml_tests_metadata.csv.
    • Correctness Verification: 100% coverage invariant asserted across 8 unit tests in J_softeng/tests/test_main.cpp.
